opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. FunSearch was really an important proof of concept. It showed that if you pair a large language model with an automated evaluator, you can search through the space of programs and find genuinely new things. We used it on the cap set problem in combinatorics and on bin packing heuristics, and it found constructions that went beyond what people had known. But FunSearch was quite constrained. It typically evolved a single, fairly short function, the "priority" function or a heuristic, inside a fixed skeleton that we wrote. And it relied on relatively small models generating huge numbers of samples.

AlphaEvolve takes that core idea and scales it along several dimensions at once. First, instead of evolving one small function, it can evolve entire codebases: multiple functions, hundreds of lines, across different components of a system. That changes the kind of problem you can attack. Second, it uses much more capable Gemini models, an ensemble where a faster model gives you breadth of ideas and a stronger model gives you depth and higher-quality suggestions. Third, the evolutionary machinery is richer. The model sees prior programs, their scores, and context about the problem, and it proposes diffs, targeted edits, rather than writing from scratch each time. And it can optimize multiple metrics at once.

The result is that it's not just a tool for a specific math puzzle; it's much more general. On the mathematical side, we ran it on over fifty open problems across analysis, geometry, and combinatorics. In most cases it rediscovered the best known constructions, and in a meaningful fraction it actually improved on them, things like the kissing number problem in eleven dimensions. Probably the result that got the most attention was matrix multiplication: it found a way to multiply four-by-four complex-valued matrices using forty-eight scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's 1969 algorithm in that setting. That's notable because AlphaTensor, a system purpose-built for that problem, hadn't found it. A general-purpose coding agent did.

And then there's the practical side, which I think is equally exciting. We deployed it inside Google's own infrastructure. It found a scheduling heuristic for our data centers, Borg, that recovers on average about seven-tenths of a percent of fleet-wide compute resources, which at Google's scale is enormous. It sped up a key kernel in Gemini's own training, which is a nice sort of recursive story: the AI helping make the training of the AI more efficient. It even contributed to hardware design, proposing simplifications to circuits for TPUs.

So the big shift, I'd say, is from "an LLM can find a clever function for a narrow problem" to "an LLM-driven evolutionary agent can be a general engine for scientific and algorithmic discovery," as long as you have a way to evaluate solutions automatically. That evaluator is the key constraint, and it's also where the human expertise really matters: deciding what to measure, what problems are worth posing. The system then explores in ways people wouldn't, and often comes back with solutions that are both surprising and, importantly, interpretable, because they're code you can read and verify.

r001.rationale: It says FunSearch used a fixed skeleton and AlphaEvolve can evolve entire codebases, but does not clearly state that AlphaEvolve removes the researcher-supplied template constraint.

r002.rationale: It contrasts FunSearch evolving a single short function with AlphaEvolve evolving entire codebases across multiple functions and components.

r003.rationale: It mentions more capable models and FunSearch generating many samples, but does not state that AlphaEvolve uses fewer function evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that FunSearch was a proof of concept, and AlphaEvolve is the thing we actually wanted to build all along.

With FunSearch, we showed that you could pair a language model with an evaluator in an evolutionary loop and discover things that humans hadn't found, like the cap set constructions. But it was quite constrained. You were evolving a single function, usually a small heuristic, in a fairly narrow setting. The model was essentially filling in one blank in a template, and the search was happening in a very limited space.

AlphaEvolve lifts a lot of those constraints. First, it operates on entire codebases rather than a single function. The model can propose changes across many components of a program, which means the space of algorithms it can express is much richer. Second, we're using much more capable models, the Gemini family, and the quality of each proposal is dramatically better. In FunSearch, most candidates were noise and you relied on the evaluator to filter. Now the model is reasoning about why something might work, and a much larger fraction of its proposals are genuinely plausible.

The third piece, and I think this is underappreciated, is the flexibility of the evaluation. Any problem where you can write a program that scores a candidate solution is fair game. That's what let us go from pure mathematics to things like the matrix multiplication result, where we found an algorithm for four by four complex matrices that improved on Strassen's bound from the 1960s, and then to very practical problems inside Google, like scheduling in our data centers or optimising kernels for training Gemini itself. That last one is a nice loop: the system is helping make the models that power it faster.

The thing I'm most excited about, though, is not any single result. It's that we have a general-purpose discovery engine where the human contribution shifts to framing the problem well and writing a good evaluator. If you can do that, the system can explore far more broadly than a person could, and it comes back with things that are verifiably correct. That combination, open-ended search plus rigorous verification, is what I think takes us from automating a trick to actually accelerating science.

r001.rationale: It describes FunSearch as filling in a template and says AlphaEvolve lifts that constraint by operating across entire codebases, clearly conveying a broader search without the same template restriction.

r002.rationale: It directly contrasts FunSearch evolving a single function with AlphaEvolve proposing changes across an entire codebase.

r003.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve produces a larger fraction of plausible proposals, but does not state that it discovers algorithms using fewer function evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key advance is the scope of what you can search over. With FunSearch, we showed that a language model, combined with an evaluator and an evolutionary search process, could discover useful new programs. AlphaEvolve takes that idea further, toward evolving more substantial algorithms rather than just a small function within a fixed template.

The important thing is that the model proposes a change, but it doesn’t get to decide whether that change is an improvement. We run the code, check correctness, and measure performance. The successful candidates then inform the next round of proposals. That feedback loop lets us turn the model’s creativity into progress we can verify.

So the opportunity is to move from solving a narrowly specified puzzle to improving algorithms used in real computational systems. The constraint is that you still need a reliable evaluator: you have to be able to say what success means and test it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions FunSearch’s fixed template but does not state that AlphaEvolve removes the requirement for a researcher-supplied template.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AlphaEvolve evolving more substantial algorithms with FunSearch discovering a small function within a fixed template.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the number of function evaluations or claim that AlphaEvolve needs fewer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is from discovering a clever function within an algorithm to being able to evolve much larger pieces of the algorithm itself. With FunSearch, you have a language model proposing code and an evaluator checking whether that code improves the solution. AlphaEvolve takes that feedback loop further, allowing a broader search over more complex programs.

That matters because an improvement may require several parts of an algorithm to change together. You want the system to propose those changes, test them, and build on the candidates that work. The evaluator is crucial: the model can suggest something that looks elegant, but we need to establish that it is correct and actually better.

So I see this as moving toward a more general tool for algorithm discovery, where human researchers define the problem and the criteria for success, and the system helps explore the space of possible solutions.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broader search but does not state that AlphaEvolve removes FunSearch’s researcher-supplied template constraint.

r002.rationale: It contrasts FunSearch discovering a clever function within an algorithm with AlphaEvolve evolving larger pieces of the algorithm itself.

r003.rationale: It mentions evaluation and feedback, but makes no claim that AlphaEvolve discovers algorithms using fewer function evaluations than FunSearch.
